severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Chronic inflammatory condition with episodic flare-ups)
possible_causes: Genetic predisposition affecting skin barrier function (e.g., filaggrin gene mutations)
Immune system hyperreactivity
Environmental triggers (harsh soaps, detergents, allergens, cold/dry weather)
Emotional stress and anxiety
Hormonal fluctuations
common_symptoms: Intense itching (pruritus), often worsening at night
Dry, red to brownish-gray patches on skin (commonly on hands, feet, inner elbows, and knees)
Small, raised bumps that may leak fluid and crust over when scratched
Thickened, cracked, or scaly skin (lichenification)
Raw, sensitive skin from scratching
treatment_suggestions: Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors to reduce inflammation
Regular application of thick emollients or barrier repair creams
Oral antihistamines to help manage severe night-time itching
Phototherapy (light therapy) for widespread or resistant cases
prevention_tips: Moisturize skin at least twice daily, especially immediately after bathing
Take short, warm (not hot) baths or showers
Use mild, fragrance-free cleansers and avoid harsh soaps
Identify and avoid personal trigger factors (e.g., wool, synthetic fabrics, specific detergents)
Keep fingernails trimmed to minimize skin damage from scratching
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a dermatologist if eczema pain interferes with sleep or daily activities, if skin becomes painful, hot, or oozes pus (signs of bacterial infection), or if home remedies fail to control flare-ups.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Contagious viral infection causing recurring painful lesions)
possible_causes: Infection with Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (oral/facial) or Type 2 (genital)
Direct contact with infected lesions, saliva, or bodily fluids
Reactivation triggers: fever, illness, stress, UV exposure, or hormonal changes
common_symptoms: Painful, fluid-filled blisters or open sores around the lips/mouth (oral) or genital area
Tingling, itching, or burning sensation prior to blister eruption (prodrome)
Blisters that break open, ooze, and form a crust
Flu-like symptoms during primary outbreak (fever, swollen lymph nodes, body aches)
treatment_suggestions: Prescription oral antiviral medications (e.g., acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) to shorten duration and frequency
Topical antiviral creams or protective ointments
Over-the-counter pain relievers (ibuprofen, acetaminophen) to manage discomfort
Cool compresses applied to external sores
prevention_tips: Avoid direct physical contact (kissing, sexual activity) during active outbreaks or prodromal symptoms
Avoid sharing personal items like towels, lip balm, or utensils during flare-ups
Use barrier protection (condoms/dental dams) during intimate contact
Apply sunscreen to lips if sunlight triggers oral outbreaks
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a physician if you experience your first outbreak, if lesions spread near the eyes, if you have a weakened immune system, or if outbreaks occur unusually frequently.

severity_estimate: Moderate (Highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection)
possible_causes: Infection by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes bacteria
Bacterial invasion through minor skin breaks, cuts, insect bites, or eczema patches
Spread through direct contact or contaminated towels, bedding, and toys
common_symptoms: Red sores that quickly rupture, ooze for a few days, and form honey-colored crusts
Fluid-filled blisters (bullous impetigo) that break open easily
Itching and mild soreness around the affected area (commonly mouth and nose)
Swollen lymph nodes near the infected area
treatment_suggestions: Topical prescription antibiotic ointments (e.g., mupirocin) for localized infection
Oral antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional for widespread lesions
Gentle washing of crusts with warm water and antibacterial soap before ointment application
prevention_tips: Practice rigorous handwashing with soap and water
Keep cuts, scrapes, and insect bites clean and covered
Avoid sharing clothes, towels, bed linens, or razors with an infected person
Wash an infected person's clothes and linens separately in hot water
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a doctor promptly for proper antibiotic prescription, or immediately if sores become increasingly painful, red, swollen, or if fever develops.

severity_estimate: Moderate to High (Chronic autoimmune disorder causing accelerated skin cell buildup)
possible_causes: Autoimmune systemic disease where T-cells attack healthy skin tissue
Genetic factors and family history
Triggers: skin injury, stress, streptococcal infections, cold weather, smoking, or certain medications
common_symptoms: Thick red patches of skin covered with silvery, metallic scales (plaque psoriasis)
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed or itch intensely
Burning, soreness, or stiffness in joints (psoriatic arthritis)
Pitted, thickened, or discolored nails
treatment_suggestions: Topical therapies: corticosteroids, synthetic vitamin D analogs, coal tar, or retinoids
Phototherapy (UV light exposure under medical supervision)
Systemic medications and biological therapies (biologics) for moderate to severe cases
prevention_tips: Keep skin well-moisturized with thick creams or ointments
Avoid known personal triggers such as excessive stress, alcohol, and smoking
Protect skin from trauma, cuts, or severe sunburns (Koebner phenomenon)
Maintain a healthy weight and balanced lifestyle
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a dermatologist if psoriasis covers significant body surface area, causes severe discomfort or joint pain, or fails to respond to topical over-the-counter care.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Acute inflammatory skin response to irritants or allergens)
possible_causes: Contact with allergic triggers (poison ivy, nickel, latex, cosmetics, fragrances)
Exposure to chemical irritants (harsh soaps, solvents, bleach)
Viral or bacterial systemic infections
Adverse drug reactions
common_symptoms: Redness, inflammation, and localized skin warmth
Itching, stinging, or burning sensation
Small bumps, hives, or fluid-filled blisters
Dry, scaly, or flaking skin patches
treatment_suggestions: Wash affected area with mild soap and water to remove offending irritants
Over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream to reduce localized inflammation
Calamine lotion or cool damp compresses to soothe itching
Oral antihistamines for allergic itching relief
prevention_tips: Identify and avoid contact with known allergens and chemical irritants
Wear protective gloves when handling household chemicals or gardening
Perform patch testing before using new cosmetics or skincare products
Use hypoallergenic and unscented skin products
when_to_see_a_doctor: Seek immediate emergency care if a rash spreads rapidly across the body, is accompanied by difficulty breathing, facial swelling, high fever, or blisters/sores in the eyes or mouth.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Contagious fungal skin infection)
possible_causes: Infection by dermatophyte fungi (e.g., Trichophyton, Microsporum)
Direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected person or animal (pets like cats/dogs)
Contact with contaminated objects, sports equipment, or moist surfaces (gym floors, pool decks)
common_symptoms: Circular, ring-shaped red rash with raised, slightly scaly borders and clear skin in center
Itching, irritation, and mild burning at the rash site
Expanding circular rings that may merge together
treatment_suggestions: Over-the-counter topical antifungal creams (e.g., clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine)
Prescription-strength topical or oral antifungal medications for widespread or stubborn cases
prevention_tips: Keep skin dry and clean, especially skin folds, groin, and feet
Avoid sharing personal items like towels, clothing, hairbrushes, or athletic gear
Wear footwear in public showers, locker rooms, and pool areas
Have pets evaluated by a veterinarian if they display patches of hair loss
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a doctor if the ringworm rash does not improve after 2 weeks of OTC antifungal treatment, spreads significantly, or becomes red, hot, and oozing.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Chronic facial vascular condition with periodic flushing)
possible_causes: Vascular reactivity and abnormal facial blood vessel regulation
Immune system dysregulation and microscopic Demodex mite overgrowth
Genetic factors
Triggers: spicy foods, hot beverages, alcohol, extreme temperatures, sun, stress
common_symptoms: Persistent redness and flushing across central face (cheeks, nose, chin, forehead)
Visible broken blood vessels (telangiectasia)
Swollen red bumps and pus-filled pimples resembling acne
Burning, stinging sensation on facial skin
Eye irritation, redness, or swollen eyelids (ocular rosacea)
treatment_suggestions: Topical medications (brimonidine, azelaic acid, metronidazole, ivermectin)
Oral antibiotics (e.g., low-dose doxycycline) for anti-inflammatory action
Laser or intense pulsed light (IPL) therapy to reduce visible red vessels
prevention_tips: Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+) daily
Identify and avoid individual dietary and environmental lifestyle triggers
Use gentle, non-abrasive skincare products without alcohol or harsh exfoliants
Protect face from cold wind with scarves or masks
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a dermatologist if persistent facial redness causes physical discomfort, emotional distress, or if eyes feel gritty, dry, or inflamed.

severity_estimate: Moderate (Highly contagious parasitic infestation requiring prompt treatment)
possible_causes: Infestation by microscopic human itch mites (*Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*)
Direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact with an infected individual
Transmission through shared clothing, bedding, or towels (less common)
common_symptoms: Intense, debilitating itching, particularly severe at night
Thin, irregular burrow tracks made of tiny bumps or blisters on the skin
Common sites: finger webs, wrists, elbows, armpits, waist, buttocks, and knees
Secondary bacterial skin infections from vigorous scratching
treatment_suggestions: Prescription topical scabicide creams (e.g., 5% Permethrin cream applied neck down overnight)
Oral prescription medication (Ivermectin) for crusted scabies or large outbreaks
Antihistamines or mild topical steroids to relieve post-treatment itching
prevention_tips: Treat all household members and close physical contacts simultaneously
Wash all bedding, towels, and worn clothing in hot water and dry on high heat
Seal non-washable items in plastic bags for at least 3 to 7 days to starve mites
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a physician immediately if you suspect scabies for prescription scabicide treatment, or if treated skin shows signs of bacterial infection (pus, increasing redness).

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Non-contagious autoimmune disorder causing depigmentation)
possible_causes: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (pigment-producing skin cells)
Genetic factors and family history of autoimmune diseases
Oxidative stress, neurogenic factors, or severe skin trauma (sunburn/cuts)
common_symptoms: Patchy loss of skin color resulting in milky-white macules and patches
Premature whitening or graying of hair on scalp, eyelashes, eyebrows, or beard
Loss of color in tissues lining the inside of mouth and nose (mucous membranes)
Symmetrical distribution of white patches across both sides of the body
treatment_suggestions: Topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus)
Targeted phototherapy (Narrowband UVB) to stimulate repigmentation
Oral JAK inhibitors or topical ruxolitinib as prescribed by a specialist
Depigmentation therapy (for extensive vitiligo) or cosmetic camouflage creams
prevention_tips: Vitiligo cannot be prevented; mitigate progression by avoiding skin injuries/friction
Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen diligently to depigmented patches to prevent severe sunburn
Minimize physical trauma to skin (cuts, scrapes, tight clothing)
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a dermatologist if you notice sudden white patches forming on skin or hair to confirm diagnosis and begin early repigmentation therapies.

severity_estimate: Mild to Moderate (Very common inflammatory pilosebaceous disorder)
possible_causes: Excessive sebum (oil) production driven by androgenic hormones
Hyperkeratinization leading to clogged hair follicles/pores
Overgrowth of *Cutibacterium acnes* bacteria within pores
Dietary factors, high stress levels, and friction/pressure on skin
common_symptoms: Comedones: open (blackheads) and closed (whiteheads)
Inflammatory papules (small red bumps) and pustules (pimples with pus)
Nodules and deep, painful fluid-filled cysts (cystic acne)
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or permanent scarring
treatment_suggestions: Over-the-counter topical treatments: Salicylic acid, Benzoyl peroxide, or Adapalene gel
Prescription topical or oral antibiotics, topical retinoids (tretinoin, trifarotene)
Hormonal therapy (oral contraceptives, spironolactone) for females
Oral Isotretinoin for severe, recalcitrant, or scarring cystic acne
prevention_tips: Wash face twice daily with a non-comedogenic cleanser
Avoid picking, squeezing, or popping acne lesions to prevent scarring and infection
Choose oil-free and non-comedogenic skincare and makeup products
Shampoo oily hair regularly and keep hair away from the face
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a dermatologist if OTC products fail after 6 to 8 weeks, if acne produces deep painful cysts, or if lesions begin causing permanent scars or emotional distress.

severity_estimate: High (Potentially serious deep bacterial skin infection requiring urgent medical attention)
possible_causes: Bacterial invasion into deep dermis and subcutaneous tissues (commonly *Streptococcus* or *Staphylococcus*)
Entry points through cuts, puncture wounds, surgical sites, ulcers, athlete's foot, or animal bites
Venous insufficiency or lymphedema causing localized fluid accumulation
common_symptoms: Rapidly spreading red, swollen, warm, and tender skin area
Severe pain and tightness in affected limb/body area
Fever, chills, fatigue, and cold sweats
Red streaks radiating from the infection site or blistering
treatment_suggestions: Prompt course of oral antibiotics prescribed by a physician
Intravenous (IV) antibiotics in hospital settings for severe or rapidly spreading cases
Elevation of the affected limb to reduce swelling
Rest and pain management
prevention_tips: Clean all skin wounds, cuts, and scrapes immediately with soap and water and apply antibiotic ointment
Keep wounds clean and covered with sterile bandages
Treat underlying skin conditions like fungal athlete's foot promptly to maintain intact skin
Inspect feet daily if living with diabetes or poor peripheral circulation
when_to_see_a_doctor: Seek emergency medical care immediately if skin becomes rapidly red, swollen, hot, and painful, or if accompanied by high fever, red streaks, confusion, or dizziness.

disease_name: Dark Spots / Hyperpigmentation (Melasma, Post-Inflammatory, Solar Lentigines)
severity_estimate: Mild (Cosmetic concern caused by excess melanin production)
possible_causes: Overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) sunlight and visible light
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) following acne, eczema, or skin trauma
Hormonal changes (pregnancy, birth control pills, hormone therapy in Melasma)
Natural skin aging (age spots / liver spots)
common_symptoms: Flat dark brown, tan, or grayish spots or patches on skin
Uneven skin tone and hyperpigmented areas on sun-exposed zones (face, hands, shoulders)
Symmetrical facial patches across forehead, cheeks, and upper lip
treatment_suggestions: Topical lightening agents: Hydroquinone, Azelaic acid, Vitamin C, Kojic acid, Niacinamide, or Tranexamic acid
Topical retinoids (tretinoin) to accelerate cell turnover
Professional chemical peels, microdermabrasion, or laser/IPL therapy under specialist supervision
prevention_tips: Wear broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen daily, year-round, reapplying every 2 hours outdoors
Wear protective hats and sun-protective clothing
Treat inflammatory skin conditions (like acne) early without picking or scratching lesions
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a dermatologist for targeted clinical treatments, or seek immediate evaluation if any dark spot changes shape, color, or border, bleeds, or grows rapidly (rule out melanoma).

possible_causes: N/A - Standard healthy skin structure with balanced hydration and intact barrier function
common_symptoms: Even skin texture and natural barrier integrity without active inflammation
Absence of unexplained lesions, severe itching, scaling, or purulent discharge
Comfortable, adequately hydrated, and supple skin tone
treatment_suggestions: No medical or corrective treatment required
Maintain consistent daily preventive skincare routine
prevention_tips: Cleanse gently daily with a mild cleanser
Apply daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen
Moisturize according to skin type (dry, normal, oily, combination)
Stay adequately hydrated and eat a balanced diet rich in vitamins and essential fatty acids
when_to_see_a_doctor: Schedule an annual routine skin check with a dermatologist, or seek medical advice if any new spots, moles, rashes, or skin changes develop.

disease_name: Skin Cancer (Melanoma, Basal Cell Carcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma)
severity_estimate: High to Critical (Malignant cellular growth requiring immediate medical diagnosis and treatment)
possible_causes: DNA damage in skin cells caused by cumulative or severe blistering UV radiation (sunlight/tanning beds)
Fair skin tone, light hair, blue eyes, or tendency to burn easily
Family or personal history of skin cancer or high mole count
Immunosuppression or exposure to ionizing radiation/chemicals
common_symptoms: ABCDEs of Melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolving shape/size
Pearly, flesh-colored, or waxy bump (Basal Cell Carcinoma)
Firm red nodule or flat scaly, crusted lesion (Squamous Cell Carcinoma)
Sore that does not heal, bleeds spontaneously, or crusts repeatedly
treatment_suggestions: Surgical excision, Mohs micrographic surgery, or curettage and electrodessication
Immunotherapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy for advanced/metastatic disease
prevention_tips: Avoid tanning beds and mid-day sun exposure (10 AM to 4 PM)
Use broad-spectrum SPF 30+ water-resistant sunscreen daily
Wear UV-blocking clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and UV-filtering sunglasses
Perform monthly self-examinations of skin from head to toe
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a dermatologist immediately if you notice a new mole, an evolving spot, a sore that fails to heal within 4 weeks, or any lesion following the ABCDE criteria.

severity_estimate: Mild to High (Vascular reaction that can be acute or chronic, potentially linked to anaphylaxis)
possible_causes: Allergic reaction to foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs), medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs), or insect stings
Physical triggers: pressure, heat, cold, exercise, or vibration (physical urticaria)
Viral or bacterial infections
Emotional stress
common_symptoms: Raised, intensely itchy red or skin-colored welts (wheals) with clear borders
Welts that appear rapidly, change shape, fade, and reappear elsewhere in hours
Blanching (center turns white when pressed)
Swelling under the skin (angioedema), often around eyelids or lips
treatment_suggestions: Non-drowsy second-generation oral H1 antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine)
Short courses of oral corticosteroids for severe acute episodes
Injectable epinephrine (EpiPen) if hives are part of a severe allergic reaction/anaphylaxis
prevention_tips: Identify and avoid known food, drug, or environmental allergens
Avoid tight-fitting clothing that creates high friction or pressure on skin
Apply cool compresses and avoid hot baths during flare-ups
when_to_see_a_doctor: Seek EMERGENCY medical care immediately if hives occur with difficulty breathing, throat tightness, tongue/lip swelling, or dizziness. Consult a doctor if hives persist beyond 6 weeks (chronic urticaria).

severity_estimate: Mild (Natural physiological aging process of skin)
possible_causes: Intrinsic natural aging (gradual reduction in collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid synthesis)
Extrinsic photoaging (UV radiation breakdown of dermal structural matrix)
Repetitive facial muscular expressions (dynamic lines)
Cigarette smoking and environmental pollution exposure
Dehydration and sleep position friction
common_symptoms: Fine lines around eyes (crow's feet), mouth, and forehead
Deeper furrows and folds (nasolabial folds, marionette lines)
Loss of skin firmness, elasticity, and volume
Sagging skin along jawline and neck
treatment_suggestions: Topical retinoids (tretinoin, retinol) to stimulate collagen production
Hydrating agents like hyaluronic acid serums and peptide creams
Cosmetic procedures: Neuromodulators (Botox), dermal fillers, microneedling, laser resurfacing, or chemical peels
prevention_tips: Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen every day, regardless of weather
Maintain a healthy skincare routine with antioxidants (Vitamin C) and rich moisturizers
Avoid smoking and excessive alcohol consumption
Stay well-hydrated and wear sunglasses to prevent squinting
when_to_see_a_doctor: Consult a board-certified dermatologist or cosmetic specialist if you desire safe, professional advice on anti-aging regimens, topical prescription retinoids, or minimally invasive cosmetic procedures.
